extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and readers interested in philosophy of science and the logic/method of scientific concepts
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the status, usefulness, and limits of scientific conceptions (e.g., geometry, atom, ether, continuity/discontinuity) as presented in a philosophy-of-science textbook. Focuses on empirical grounding, explanatory/predictive power, economy of thought, and limits of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity as predictive/codifying power
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of geometrical and scientific conceptions 'lies in the power they give us of codifying past and predicting future experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a test: a conception is valuable if it enables effective classification of past sense-impressions and reliable prediction of future ones. Example: geometry does not correspond exactly to perception but is valid insofar as it lets us classify and predict within the keenness of our senses and instruments. Anti-pattern: treating a conception as valid because it is elegant or intuitively appealing despite lacking classificatory/predictive utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions as shorthand / economy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific conceptions (atom, ether, geometrical surface) are 'shorthand methods' for distinguishing, classifying, and resuming phases of sense-impression; their value is their economy of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge conceptions by how much they simplify and compress complex correlations and sequences of sense-impressions. Guidance: retain a conception while it 'economizes' thought; replace or extend it when it ceases to do so. Example: atom and molecule reduce complexity of phenomena and enable formulation of wide-reaching laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding / refusal to project beyond perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientist 'refuses to project his conceptions, atom and ether, into the real world of perception until he has perceived them there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat theoretical entities as conceptual tools unless and until they form persistent groups of sense-impressions or are directly observed by experiment. Anti-pattern: asserting the real existence of 'things-in-themselves' (metaphysical projection) on the basis of theory alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose models by explanatory/practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between incompatible conceptions (e.g., continuous boundaries vs. atomic structure) by which conception 'would enable us to classify and describe phenomena better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the model that best fits the methods and phenomena you wish to describe. Example: physicists prefer discontinuity (atomistic view) because it explains elasticity, compression, temperature, pressure, and emission/absorption phenomena. Anti-pattern: retaining a conception despite inferior explanatory utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of applicability / conditional validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific conceptions are valid only within certain ranges: 'Geometry enables us to predict with absolute certainty ... when these impressions do not involve more than a certain keenness in our senses, more than a certain degree of exactness in our measuring instruments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories with respect to the empirical scale and precision where they apply. Treat laws and conceptions as approximations or averages, not absolute truths for all perceptual scales. When observations exceed the limits, modify or extend concepts rather than declaring prior concepts wholly false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental support expands conceptual validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments (e.g., Hertz's) 'immensely increased the validity of the scientific concept, ether, by showing that a wider range of perceptual experience may be described in terms of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater credence to conceptions that acquire experimental support demonstrating broader descriptive/predictive reach. Note the distinction: experimental support increases validity as a concept even if it does not logically prove perceptual existence. Example: Hertz's work increased confidence in ether as a useful concept without making it a direct perceptual object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual detectability as criterion for perceptual reality
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'real existence' is meant that a conception 'forms a more or less permanent group of sense-impressions.' If it does not, it remains a conception rather than a perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use permanence and detectability in sense-impressions as the criterion for elevating a concept to perceptual reality. Example: ether lacks grouped sense-impressions and so is better treated as a concept; nerves are both conduits and perceptually evident and so can be treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical claims beyond sense-impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Science 'asserts no perceptual reality for its own shorthand' and should not claim knowledge of the world beyond sense-impression; metaphysical 'things-in-themselves' are outside scientific claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique or reject attempts to convert functional, classificatory concepts into ultimate metaphysical explanations. Leave purely metaphysical speculations to metaphysicians; within science, focus on descriptions of sense-impressions and their correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept formation by extending perceptual processes to limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Many scientific concepts arise 'by carrying to a limit in conception processes which have no such limit in perception' (e.g., continuity, atom, ether are conceived by extending perceptual comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conceptual limits are imaginative extrapolations suggested by perception; treat such concepts as heuristic tools. Use this understanding to justify both the utility and the tentative status of such concepts; be ready to revise when new perceptual evidence or instruments change the relevant scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification and extension of concepts with increasing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: As knowledge grows and the senses become keener, 'we are compelled to widen our concepts, or to add additional ones' — original concepts are not usually invalidated but form a basis for limited classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor incremental modification/extension of existing conceptions to accommodate new phenomena rather than wholesale rejection unless necessary. Example: Euclidean geometry may remain valid for a wide range of perceptions even if new geometries are needed at other scales.
